opus-5.5.text:
It's something I've thought about a lot, and I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but with a lot of emphasis on the "cautiously." Agriculture is one of those areas where people assume that because robots have transformed manufacturing, they'll just naturally sweep into farming too. But farming is fundamentally different. A factory is a structured environment: you control the lighting, the positions of parts, the timing. A field is the opposite. Every plant is different, the lighting changes minute to minute, there's wind, there's mud, leaves occlude the fruit you're trying to reach. And produce is delicate; a strawberry or a tomato bruises if you grip it wrong.

So harvesting in particular has been a remarkably hard problem. There have been many startups over the years trying to build strawberry pickers, apple pickers and so on, and a lot of them have struggled or folded. The perception problem of finding the fruit, judging whether it's ripe and figuring out how to approach it without damaging the plant is still very challenging, and then the manipulation, actually grasping and detaching it reliably and quickly enough to compete economically with skilled human pickers, is harder still. Human pickers are incredibly fast and adaptable.

Where I see more near-term promise is in tasks that are a bit more forgiving. Things like weeding, precision spraying, monitoring plant health with cameras and sensors, and targeted pruning. Some of my own work has looked at polyculture gardening, where you grow many different plant species close together, which is actually better for the soil and reduces pests, but is very labor-intensive for humans to manage. We built a system called AlphaGarden to explore whether a robot with a camera overhead could learn to water and prune a polyculture garden. What we found is that it's possible to get it to work reasonably well, but it's humbling. The plants don't follow your models; nature is very good at surprising you.

Indoor and vertical farming is another area where robots can make real headway, because you get to bring back some of that structure: controlled lighting, standardized trays, predictable plant positions. That's kind of the trick in robotics generally: when the world is too messy, you try to restructure the environment to meet the robot halfway.

So my overall assessment is that we'll see steady, incremental progress, with robots taking on specific tasks and working alongside farmworkers rather than some sudden replacement of human labor. I'm always a little wary of the hype cycle. People see an impressive demo video and extrapolate, but that demo may have taken fifty tries, and getting from 80 percent reliability to 99 percent is where most of the hard work lies. I think the real story will be a gradual one, and that's okay. Labor shortages in agriculture are real, so there's genuine value in robots that can help, even if they're not doing everything.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but I want to be careful, because agriculture is one of those domains where people have been predicting robots are just around the corner for a very long time, and the reality keeps turning out to be harder than anyone expected.

Let me separate the two parts of your question, growing and harvesting, because they're really quite different problems.

Growing, in the sense of monitoring and tending plants, is actually where I think there's been genuine progress. If you look at what's happening in greenhouses, in vertical farms, in some of the larger outdoor operations, you have robots and automated systems doing irrigation, doing imaging, tracking plant health, doing targeted weeding. Some of these use computer vision to distinguish a crop from a weed and then zap the weed with a laser or a micro-dose of herbicide. That's a real thing. It's working in the field. The reason it works is that it's largely a perception and navigation problem, and the physical action required is fairly simple. You don't have to touch the plant.

Harvesting is the hard part, and it's hard for reasons that come back to something I've spent most of my career on, which is grasping. A ripe strawberry or a tomato is delicate, it's irregular, it's partially occluded by leaves, it's a slightly different shape and color every single time, and you have to detach it without bruising it and without damaging the plant. Humans do this effortlessly. They do it with their eyes half closed, in conversation, at a rate of one every second or two. For a robot, every one of those steps is a challenge. The perception is uncertain, the lighting outdoors is terrible and changes constantly, and the physics of a soft object being pulled off a stem is surprisingly hard to model.

So we have a situation where there are many prototypes, lots of companies, and a handful that are actually operating commercially, mostly on crops that are more robot-friendly, like apples, where the fruit is firm and the orchards can be trained into flat walls. Strawberries and tomatoes have been the holy grail for about fifteen years, and we're still not there at scale.

I think there's an economic dimension that gets overlooked. In many places the motivation for these robots isn't that they're cheaper than human labor. It's that the labor isn't available. Farmers in California and elsewhere will tell you they literally cannot find enough people at harvest time, and crops rot in the field. That changes the calculus. A robot that's slower and more expensive than a skilled picker can still be worth deploying if the alternative is losing the crop. So I think the demand pull is real.

My honest assessment is that over the next decade we'll see these systems become common for a subset of crops, particularly in controlled environments where you can engineer away a lot of the variability. For the open field, with messy, delicate produce, I think it's going to take longer than the enthusiasts say, and I'd be skeptical of anyone claiming a general-purpose harvesting robot is imminent. And I'd add one thing I always say about robotics, which is that even when these systems arrive, they tend to work alongside humans rather than replace them. The human handles the edge cases, the robot handles the repetitive middle. That's probably the shape of farming for a long time to come.

astra-6.text:
I think agriculture is a very promising area for robotics, but it’s useful to distinguish between the different tasks. Driving a tractor through a field is quite different from picking a ripe strawberry. With the strawberry, you have to find it among the leaves, determine whether it’s ripe, and grasp it without damaging it—or the plant. And you have to do that quickly enough to make economic sense.

That’s one of the fascinating things about robotics: things that seem effortless to a human can be extraordinarily difficult for a machine. The plants aren’t all in exactly the same position. The lighting changes. The fruit varies in shape and firmness.

So I’m optimistic, especially where you can structure the environment to make the robot’s job easier. But I’d expect progress task by task, crop by crop, rather than a general-purpose robot that can walk onto any farm and do everything. There’s a lot of room for useful automation well before we get to that point.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, particularly about robots working in greenhouses, where you can control the environment and arrange the plants to make them easier to reach. Out in a field, you have changing weather, lighting, and terrain, and every plant looks a little different. That makes the problem much harder.

Harvesting is especially interesting because it combines perception with manipulation. You have to find the fruit, determine whether it’s ripe, and then pick it without bruising it or damaging the plant. Something that seems very simple to a person can be quite difficult for a robot.

So I expect progress crop by crop, rather than one general-purpose robot that can grow and harvest everything. There are real opportunities, but getting a system to work reliably and economically is a much higher bar than giving a successful demonstration.
